docs.title: Days out
docs.text: days_out, days to session, lead time Number of days between today and the session date. Every fill curve is indexed by days out, from 365 down to 0.  A session on 1 July viewed on 1 June is 30 days out.

docs.title: Fill rate
docs.text: utilization, occupancy, slot utilization Appointments divided by the session's appointment slots (capacity). fill_rate = net_appointments / capacity 2,400 kept appointments in a 3,000-slot session is a fill rate of 80%.

docs.title: Fill curve
docs.text: pace curve, fill pace Cumulative appointments plotted against days out. Comparing a session's curve with similar past sessions shows whether it is ahead or behind.

docs.title: Segment
docs.text: cluster, demand segment Group of sessions with similar booking behaviour (reach x season x length, for example local / flu season / one-day). Benchmarks are built per segment.

docs.title: Target curve
docs.text: target pace, target fill rate, strategic target The pace a session should be at for each day out, taken from the 60th percentile of similar past sessions. Targets never go down as the session gets closer - a running maximum stops a noisy day from lowering the bar. target_fill(days_out) = running max of P60(fill rate of past sessions at days_out)

docs.title: Glide path
docs.text: tactical target, path to target Day-by-day route from today's appointments to the final target, shaped like appointments normally arrive rather than a straight line. Unlike the target curve, it starts from where the session actually is today. glide(days_out) = net_today + (target_final - net_today) * progress(days_out)

docs.title: Share of final
docs.text: distribution, normalized curve, percent of final Share of a session's final appointments already booked at a given day out (a 0 to 1 curve). share_of_final(days_out) = net_appointments(days_out) / net_appointments(0)

docs.title: Pickup projection
docs.text: projection, forecast, projected final Estimate of final appointments from today's appointments and the typical share of final at today's day out, blended with the segment's typical final fill rate early in the window (credibility weighting). projected_final = w * net_today / median_share + (1 - w) * median_final_fill * capacity

docs.title: Credibility weight
docs.text: credibility, blending weight How much the projection trusts the session's own pickup versus history. It grows from 0 to 1 as the typical share of final reaches 30%. w = min(median_share / 0.30, 1)

docs.title: Gap to target
docs.text: shortfall, appointments short Target appointments at the session minus projected final appointments, never negative. This is the amount that must come from outreach.

docs.title: Gap to full
docs.text: unused slots, empty slots Capacity minus projected final appointments.

docs.title: Pace gap today
docs.text: behind pace, pace gap Target appointments for today minus appointments today. Positive means behind.

docs.title: Outreach units
docs.text: outreach, extra appointments, incremental demand Extra appointments that must come from outreach (reminder campaigns, waitlist calls, partner referrals) to close the gap to target, allocated over the remaining weeks.

docs.title: Baseline strategy
docs.text: baseline allocation Spreads the gap in proportion to how appointments normally arrive. Stable and low risk.

docs.title: Milestones strategy
docs.text: front-loaded allocation, milestones Front-loads the gap using checkpoints - 50% of the gap closed after 25% of the remaining time and 80% after 50%. Faster, but with more execution risk.

docs.title: Gross appointments
docs.text: gross Appointments including those that will later cancel.

docs.title: Net appointments
docs.text: net, kept appointments Appointments after cancellations - who is expected to actually show up.

docs.title: Survival rate
docs.text: net to gross, cancellation rate, cancel rate, show-up rate Median share of gross appointments that remain on the day of the session, by segment and day out. One minus survival is the expected cancellation rate. survival(days_out) = median(net_appointments / gross_appointments)

docs.title: Snapshot-first
docs.text: history snapshot, snapshot Copy the current table into history before a pipeline overwrites it, so every past version can be compared. Identical same-day snapshots are replaced, not duplicated.

docs.title: Validation gate
docs.text: publish gate, gate A check that blocks publishing when projections move more than a set threshold (5%) since the last run, so a bad input can't silently change every report.

docs.title: Control totals
docs.text: reconciliation, reconcile Checks that totals add up across steps - published rows plus rejects equal the input rows, and outreach plans add up exactly to each session's gap.

docs.title: Clinic capacity planning: fill targets, glide paths & outreach sizing - Overview
docs.text: A planning product for a clinic network's screening sessions: it turns appointment pace into targets, projections and gap-to-target, then sizes the outreach needed to close the gap, with a config-driven pipeline, SQL layer, notebook and live dashboard. Tools: Python (pandas, NumPy), SQL (Snowflake dialect), YAML config, pytest, Jupyter, JavaScript (SVG) Live demo: Interactive fill dashboard The techniques come from my professional work; the clinic network, sessions and every number are invented. ▶ Try the interactive dashboard · Open the walkthrough notebook

docs.title: Clinic capacity planning: fill targets, glide paths & outreach sizing - The setting
docs.text: A clinic network runs screening sessions (one-day clinics and multi-day drives) with a fixed number of appointment slots. Slots fill up over the months before each session, and some appointments cancel. For every upcoming session the operations team needs one trusted answer to three questions: Are we on pace? Where will we land? If we're short, how many extra appointments do we need, and when?

docs.title: Clinic capacity planning: fill targets, glide paths & outreach sizing - What the code does
docs.text: Layer Module Technique Benchmarks curves.segment_curves , 01_segment_curves.sql historical fill curves per segment (reach × season × length) from completed sessions Targets percentile target curves, curves.glide_path target trajectories plus a glide path from today's position to the session Projection & gaps curves.project_and_decompose , 02_session_plan.sql pace-to-target, projected outcome, gap-to-target and gap-to-full Outreach sizing strategies.py extra appointments needed from outreach (reminders, waitlist calls, partner referrals), allocated over time: baseline vs milestones, with eligibility rules Gross vs net gross_net.py cancellation profiles so targets reflect who actually shows up

docs.title: Clinic capacity planning: fill targets, glide paths & outreach sizing - What the code does
docs.text: Quality & governance quality.py , SQL 03 / 04 , tests/ snapshot-first runs, validation gate, reason-coded rejects, control totals Orchestration pipeline.py + config.yaml multi-step, config-driven pipeline with continue-on-failure and a run summary Decision layer export.py → live dashboard the dashboard reads data produced by the same functions as the pipeline

docs.title: Clinic capacity planning: fill targets, glide paths & outreach sizing - How it works
docs.text: Methods - Time-to-session trajectories : every metric is indexed by days (and weeks) before the session. - Percentile benchmarking : targets come from what similar sessions actually achieved (60th percentile), forced never to decrease. - Pickup projection with credibility weighting : early in the window, projections lean on history; later, on the session's own pace. - Volatility bands : ± one standard deviation of historical pace gives a low/high range, not a single number. - Gap decomposition : pace gap today , gap to target at session , gap to full . Each one maps to a different action. - Residual-demand allocation : remaining demand is spread the way appointments usually arrive, not in a straight line. - Scenario comparison : a stable baseline strategy vs a front-loaded milestone strategy, with eligibility rules (minimum gap, minimum historical support) to avoid over-allocating. - Reconciliation : every plan must add up exactly to its gap (control totals), checked in code and in SQL.

docs.title: Clinic capacity planning: fill targets, glide paths & outreach sizing - How it works
docs.text: gap to full = capacity − projected appointments at session gap to target = target appointments at session − projected appointments at session net target(days_out) = gross target(days_out) × show-up rate(days_out)

docs.title: Clinic capacity planning: fill targets, glide paths & outreach sizing - Design decisions
docs.text: Decision Why Glide paths follow how demand normally arrives, not straight lines a static target doesn't tell a team when to act A stable baseline strategy by default, milestone variants for scenarios aggressive front-loading carries more execution risk where history is thin Plan on net , not just gross cancellations make gross targets look better than reality Snapshot before every overwrite, plus a validation gate every run stays recoverable and comparable over time The dashboard reads the model's own export the picture can never drift from the numbers

docs.title: Dashboard gallery: seven interactive dashboards and the logic behind them - Overview
docs.text: Re-creations of the kinds of dashboards I build for planning, pricing and operations teams, on invented clinic-network and farm co-op data. Every number is computed by tested Python, and every page is interactive. Tools: Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy), statistics (holdout tests, Poisson models), JavaScript, SVG, Playwright, pytest Live demo: Open the gallery In my professional work I've built a whole family of dashboards, not just one. The data, names and figures here are invented; the dashboard types, questions and techniques are the ones I use.

docs.title: Dashboard gallery: seven interactive dashboards and the logic behind them - The dashboards
docs.text: Dashboard The question it answers Technique Fill pace & outreach plan Is each session on pace, where will it land, how much outreach does it need? pacing curves, credibility-weighted projection, glide paths (model) Price & performance Is revenue up because of price or volume, and where? season-to-date vs last season, price/volume decomposition, drill-down heat map Outreach effectiveness Which campaigns actually created appointments, at what cost? randomised holdouts, 95% confidence intervals, cost per incremental Market price review Where do our prices sit against the market, and can the feeds be trusted? price index, diverging heat map, feed-health checks (matching)

docs.text: Short-notice openings Which sessions in the next 14 days will have empty slots, and what to do? Poisson fill probability, no-show model, rule-based actions Group screening quote What's the lowest safe price for a block of slots? displacement pricing, interactive calculator, Monte Carlo check Comparable sessions No history for a new session: what should we plan against? weighted nearest neighbours, proxy curves

docs.title: Dashboard gallery: seven interactive dashboards and the logic behind them - Design
docs.text: - Logic in Python, drawing in the browser. builders.py computes everything and python -m dashkit build writes one data.json per dashboard. The pages only draw, so the maths can be tested. - Reuse, don't copy. The fill-pace and comparables dashboards call the capacity-planning model; the market review calls the market-prices matching pipeline. Dashboards and models can't drift apart. - Calculators run in the browser and are checked against Python. The quote and comparables pages port the Python functions to JavaScript; test_pages.py runs both on many inputs in a headless browser and requires identical results. - One chart style. Shared dash.js / dash.css : a colour-blind-checked palette in fixed order, one y-axis per chart, a tooltip on every chart, status colours used only for status, and dark mode.

docs.title: Dashboard gallery: seven interactive dashboards and the logic behind them - What the tests check
docs.text: Rule Test Grade × region totals add up to the headline; sales growth = (1 + price) × (1 + volume) − 1 test_price_performance_ Confidence intervals recomputed independently; "proven" only when the interval clears zero test_outreach_ci_and_flags Poisson tail matches SciPy test_poisson_sf_matches_scipy Displaced revenue in the quote matches a 400,000-draw simulation; more slots never displace less test_quote_ Nearest neighbours come back in distance order, exact match first test_nearest_exact_match_first_and_sorted Every page loads with no console errors; JavaScript and Python calculators agree test_pages.py

docs.title: Data knowledge assistant: catalog, glossary, lineage & grounded Q&A - Overview
docs.text: A self-service assistant for a clinic network's appointment-planning data. It answers "what is this view, where does this column live, what feeds what, what does this term mean?" from a validated catalog, with sources for every answer, as a static web app and a Python package. Tools: Python (PyYAML, networkx), information retrieval (BM25), JavaScript, GitHub Pages, Playwright, pytest Live demo: Ask the assistant The idea and techniques come from an onboarding tool I built in my professional work; the clinic catalog, glossary and data are invented. ▶ Try it in the browser , or run python -m kbassist ask "..."

docs.title: Data knowledge assistant: catalog, glossary, lineage & grounded Q&A - The setting
docs.text: A planning data product grows into many views across several layers. The knowledge needed to use them tends to live in people's heads: what grain a view has, which one holds a column, why a target never goes down, what breaks if an upstream table changes. Every question costs a senior analyst's time, and the answers aren't always the same.

docs.title: Data knowledge assistant: catalog, glossary, lineage & grounded Q&A - How it answers
docs.text: - Retrieval, not generation. Every answer is assembled from catalog entries, glossary text or a passage of a write-up, and cites them. Nothing is invented. - Synonyms from the glossary. "days_out", "days out" and "lead time" all find Days to session . Longer phrases win, so "target fill rate" is not misread as "fill rate". - Coverage-first view ranking for query help. "How do I get sessions that are behind?" prefers the view that matches both words over one that only repeats "session". - Read-only SQL. Curated example queries are shown when they exist. Otherwise a starter SELECT is built from the documented columns.

docs.title: Data knowledge assistant: catalog, glossary, lineage & grounded Q&A - One engine, two runtimes, proven equal
docs.text: The browser app is a JavaScript port of the Python package: the same tokenizer, stemmer, BM25, synonym expansion and routing. tests/test_web_parity.py serves the page, asks both versions 40 questions in a headless browser, and requires identical answer type, text, SQL and sources. The page has its own built-in check too: open the Guardrails & tests tab to see it replay the Python answers live.

docs.title: Data knowledge assistant: catalog, glossary, lineage & grounded Q&A - Where an LLM fits
docs.text: A natural next step is adding a language model to the Ask tab. The design here is the part that makes that safe: guardrails run first, retrieval selects the passages, and the model, if one is added, may only rephrase what was retrieved and must keep the citations. This public version makes no API calls, so it needs no keys and nothing leaves the browser.

docs.title: Data knowledge assistant: catalog, glossary, lineage & grounded Q&A - Adding knowledge

If the entry is incomplete, for example a missing column description or an upstream view that doesn't exist, the build stops and says exactly what to fix. Project write-ups are picked up automatically, so a new folder in professional-work/ becomes searchable on the next build.

docs.title: Market price intelligence: product matching, feed monitoring & price index - Overview
docs.text: A pipeline that tells a farm co-op where its prices sit against competing suppliers: it matches their listings to the co-op's lots, cleans a daily price feed with every common defect planted, and computes a price index that only uses data it can trust. Tools: Python (pandas, SciPy assignment, difflib), pytest The techniques come from my professional work; the co-op, competitors, products and prices are invented.

docs.title: Market price intelligence: product matching, feed monitoring & price index - The setting
docs.text: A co-op sells produce lots in four grades (Standard, Select, Premium, Organic). A market-data service delivers a daily price feed for three competing suppliers. A price comparison is only as good as two things nobody sees on a dashboard: which competitor listings count as comparable , and whether today's feed is real .

docs.title: Market price intelligence: product matching, feed monitoring & price index - The pipeline
docs.text: 1. Match listings ( matching.py ) - Grade from free text. Keyword rules first ( fancy → premium, certified → organic), then a fuzzy match to known labels for typos ( Extra Fncy → premium). Placeholders like Grade TBA are left unmapped for review , never guessed. - Comparable lots. Same region, contract length within ±1 week, harvest date within ±7 days, scored by closeness. - One-to-one assignment. For each competitor and region, the Hungarian algorithm ( scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment ) pairs listings with lots. A greedy nearest match lets one listing stand in for several lots; a test shows the difference. 2. Clean the feed ( quality.py ) Problem Detection

docs.title: Market price intelligence: product matching, feed monitoring & price index - The pipeline
docs.text: duplicates identical deliveries collapsed mixed currencies everything converted to USD typos (×10, ÷10) outlier only if both statistically extreme for that listing (robust z 6 against its rolling median) and economically implausible ( ~65% jump). The second test stops quiet listings from flagging ordinary moves. stale feed a competitor whose whole snapshot is identical to the previous day for ≥ 3 days: the provider is resending an old file. Excluded, not trusted. missing days days with no delivery, reported per competitor

docs.title: Market price intelligence: product matching, feed monitoring & price index - The pipeline
docs.text: 3. Price index ( index.py ): our price / median of matched competitors' usable prices , per lot, grade and day. A competitor's last good price is carried forward for at most 2 days. A cell needs at least 2 competitors to get an index, and gets "not enough comparables" otherwise. Positioning bands: below market ( 1.05). While Competitor B's frozen prices are excluded, the market band narrows. That's a change in who is counted , not a market move, so the daily output carries a competitors count next to every index value.

docs.title: Market price intelligence: product matching, feed monitoring & price index - Proven against planted problems
docs.text: The synthetic generator records everything it breaks. The 14 tests ( tests/ ) require the pipeline to find exactly that: every true listing match, all 40 duplicates, the 12 typo prices and no others, the 6 stale days and the 3 missing days. A market median recomputed by hand on a stale day must match the index.

docs.title: Market price intelligence: product matching, feed monitoring & price index - Proven against planted problems
docs.text: bash cd professional-work/market-prices pip install -r requirements.txt PYTHONPATH=src python -m ratekit run --out outputs --figures figures pytest -q products matched: 328 competitor products - 120 of our 120 lot-grades grade labels: 9 fixed by fuzzy match, 4 left unmapped for review feed: 40 duplicates removed, 12 outlier prices excluded stale days: {'Competitor B': 6} missing days: {'Competitor C': 3} today's positioning: above market 49, below market 37, at market 33, not enough comparables 1

docs.title: Buyer-order reconciliation & substitution bids (farm co-op) - Overview
docs.text: Daily and weekly reconciliation between a buyer marketplace and a farm co-op's invoicing system, plus an optimizer that decides which grade-substitution bids to accept. Runnable, tested, with an Excel exception report. Tools: Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy MILP), Excel automation (openpyxl, XlsxWriter), pytest The techniques come from my professional work; the farm co-op setting, data and numbers are invented.

docs.title: Buyer-order reconciliation & substitution bids (farm co-op) - The setting
docs.text: A farm co-op sells produce in grades (Standard → Choice → Select → Premium → Reserve) through a third-party buyer marketplace. A buyer holding a contract for one grade can bid a premium to receive a higher grade instead. Two systems keep the books: the marketplace records every bid and its status, and the co-op's invoicing system records what was actually charged. Reconciling them by hand is slow, because:

docs.title: Buyer-order reconciliation & substitution bids (farm co-op) - The setting
docs.text: - the marketplace export uses free-text grade labels ( "Prem." , "premium grade" , "PREMIUM" ), mixed currencies and money stored as text - bids are re-sent when they change, so the export contains duplicates - invoicing produces one file per business day : weekend activity lands in Monday's file, and on Monday morning that file often doesn't exist yet - minimum-bid price grids live in several workbooks, one tab per region, with drifting column names - every pending bid needs an accept/decline decision, and accepting uses up higher-grade produce that might otherwise sell on the spot market

docs.title: Buyer-order reconciliation & substitution bids (farm co-op) - What the code does
docs.text: Piece Module Technique Clean the marketplace export normalize.py label map with prefix fallback, money parsing, FX, keep-latest de-duplication, reason-coded rejects (never guess) Daily reconciliation reconcile.py outer join, 5 exception classes, a tolerance so rounding noise isn't flagged, control totals Missing-file fallback load_internal uses the latest business-day file and records a warning. Bids newer than that cut-off are in transit , not errors. Weekly roll-up weekly.py volume, acceptance, revenue, exception rate; partial weeks are flagged so they don't look like a drop

docs.title: Buyer-order reconciliation & substitution bids (farm co-op) - What the code does
docs.text: Combine price-grid workbooks ingest.py reads real .xlsx files, matches drifting headers through an alias table, rejects bad rows with their Excel row number Bid decisions bid_optimizer.py mixed-integer program over all pending bids, compared with the rule of thumb Reporting report.py 12-tab Excel report with a summary, filters and highlighted exceptions, plus charts Reconciliation rules Class Meaning Action written into the report CANCELLED_BUT_CHARGED marketplace says cancelled, buyer still invoiced credit the buyer; check that cancellations reach invoicing MISSING_INTERNAL accepted, the invoice file for that day exists, no charge raise the invoice; check the interface for that day

docs.title: Buyer-order reconciliation & substitution bids (farm co-op) - What the code does
docs.text: MISSING_VENDOR invoice with no marketplace record request the record or reverse PRICE_MISMATCH both sides agree, but the amount differs by more than max($0.25, 0.5%) correct to the accepted bid (FX or manual override) IN_TRANSIT accepted after the latest invoice file's cut-off timing only; re-checked next run MATCHED agrees within tolerance none Control totals prove nothing was dropped. Every bid in the union of both sources is classified exactly once, and the charged total in the detail equals the invoicing total to the cent.

docs.title: Buyer-order reconciliation & substitution bids (farm co-op) - What the code does
docs.text: Bid decisions Accepting a bid from grade A to grade B uses one unit of B and frees one unit of A . With remaining spot-market demand D ~ Poisson(λ) , the c-th remaining unit is worth spot price × P(D ≥ c) , so the cost of giving up units rises with each bid accepted on the same lot. The optimizer maximises Σ bid_i · x_i − Σ_lot,grade displacement_cost(net units used) x_i ∈ {0,1}, units used ≤ open units The displacement cost is convex and piecewise linear, so it is modelled exactly through its epigraph, and the whole problem is solved as a MILP with scipy.optimize.milp . A test checks it against brute force on a small instance. The same model gives a break-even floor for each grade path.

docs.title: Buyer-order reconciliation & substitution bids (farm co-op) - What the code does
docs.text: In the synthetic run, 387 bids are pending. The rule "accept anything at or above the grid minimum while a unit is free" accepts 312 of them and, once lost spot-market sales are counted, does worse than accepting nothing . The optimizer accepts 178, mostly into produce unlikely to sell on the spot market, and comes out about $36k ahead.

docs.title: Buyer-order reconciliation & substitution bids (farm co-op) - Run it
docs.text: bash cd professional-work/order-reconciliation pip install -r requirements.txt PYTHONPATH=src python -m orderrec run --date 2026-03-02 --out outputs/ pytest -q 27 tests run 2026-03-02 (internal cut-off 2026-02-27) ! internal file for 2026-03-02 not available; using 2026-02-27 as the latest cut-off vendor duplicates removed: 15 rejects: {'UNMAPPED_GRADE': 1, 'UNPARSEABLE_AMOUNT': 1, 'UNKNOWN_CURRENCY': 1} upload rejects: {'MIN_ABOVE_MAX': 2, 'MISSING_LOT': 2} MATCHED 686 NO_CHARGE_EXPECTED 656 IN_TRANSIT 96 PRICE_MISMATCH 29 MISSING_INTERNAL 22 CANCELLED_BUT_CHARGED 8 MISSING_VENDOR 6 revenue at risk: $18,624.78 rows reconciled: True money reconciled: True pending bids: 387 accept (rule of thumb): 312 - -15,062 accept (optimized): 178 - +35,858 expected USD

docs.title: Buyer-order reconciliation & substitution bids (farm co-op) - Run it
docs.text: The run writes the raw inputs as real files (a marketplace CSV, 19 daily invoice CSVs, two multi-tab workbooks) and reads them back. synth.py plants known problems and records them. The tests assert that the reconciliation finds exactly those problems: none missed, no false alarms, and the ±$0.02 rounding noise is not flagged. The full report is in sample_output/ .

docs.title: Buyer-order reconciliation & substitution bids (farm co-op) - Design decisions
docs.text: - Reject, don't guess. An unknown grade label or currency becomes a reason-coded reject someone can fix. - Timing is not an error. Keeping IN_TRANSIT separate from MISSING_INTERNAL stops false alarms that make people ignore the list. - Tolerance is explicit and tested. A test shows that zero tolerance would bury real mismatches under rounding noise. - Loud failures on structure, soft failures on rows. An unknown column header stops the run; a bad row is set aside. - Same scoring for every policy. The rule of thumb and the optimizer are judged with the same expected-revenue function.

docs.title: Produce pricing: elasticity, constrained price optimization & handover - Overview
docs.text: A pricing model for a farm co-op: estimates how price-sensitive each market segment and produce grade is, recommends prices within harvest volume, guardrails and a grade ladder, and comes with plain-SQL validation checks for whoever runs it next. Tools: Python (pandas, NumPy), regression (log-log OLS, empirical-Bayes shrinkage), optimization, SQL, pytest The techniques come from my professional work, including writing a model handover; the co-op setting, data and numbers are invented.

docs.title: Produce pricing: elasticity, constrained price optimization & handover - The setting
docs.text: A co-op sells four grades (Standard, Select, Premium, Organic) into four market segments (retail and wholesale, east and west). Each delivery lot has a harvest volume it can't exceed, a unit cost and a current price. The question every cycle: what price per lot and grade? The answer has to be explainable and checkable by someone who didn't build the model.

docs.title: Produce pricing: elasticity, constrained price optimization & handover - The method
docs.text: 1. Elasticity per segment and grade ( elasticity.py ) log(units) = a − e · log(price / median price) + seasonality (sin/cos of week) , fitted by OLS per cell. A cell stands on its own only with at least 30 weeks of history and a correctly signed estimate whose 95% interval excludes zero. Cells that fail are shrunk toward their grade's pooled estimate (empirical Bayes, weighted by how noisy the cell is) and labelled. The data is synthetic, so the true values are known: the chart above shows the estimates landing on them, and a test checks that shrinkage reduces the error on thin cells.

docs.title: Produce pricing: elasticity, constrained price optimization & handover - The method
docs.text: A back-test fits on all but the last 26 weeks and predicts sales at the prices actually charged: WAPE 16.9% for the model, against 31.9% for a naive same-cell average. 2. Recommended price ( optimize.py ): maximise contribution (p − cost) · min(demand(p), volume) Situation Rule elastic (e 1) closed-form optimum p = cost · e / (e − 1) inelastic (e ≤ 1) contribution keeps rising with price → go to the guardrail volume binds never price below the sell-out price: extra demand can't be supplied, so a lower price only gives money away guardrails at most ±15% per cycle

docs.title: Produce pricing: elasticity, constrained price optimization & handover - The method
docs.text: grade ladder within a lot each grade must cost ≥ 5% more than the grade below. Violations are repaired with weighted isotonic regression (pool-adjacent-violators), so the fix moves both grades as little as possible. A repair that crosses a guardrail is flagged for a person, not hidden. A test compares the closed form with a brute-force grid search on all 96 lot-grades. 3. Validation queries ( validation.py ): plain SQL that returns the rows breaking a rule, so the next owner can run them in a warehouse without the Python code: Check Fails when thin cells never used unshrunk a cell with < 30 weeks is used as its own estimate plausible elasticities an elasticity is missing, negative or 4

docs.title: Produce pricing: elasticity, constrained price optimization & handover - The method
docs.text: guardrails a price moves more than 15% without a conflict flag grade ladder a higher grade costs less than the one below (+5%) volume planned units exceed harvest volume revenue impact units_new × new price − units_now × current price doesn't recompute Tests corrupt the output on purpose and confirm that each check catches it.

docs.title: Produce pricing: elasticity, constrained price optimization & handover - Run it
docs.text: bash cd professional-work/produce-pricing pip install -r requirements.txt PYTHONPATH=src python -m pricekit run --out outputs --figures figures pytest -q 8 tests elasticity cells: 16 (3 thin cells shrunk to their grade pool) back-test WAPE: model 16.9% vs naive 31.9% recommendations: 96 lot-grades · ladder fixes 16 41 capacity binds: no lower than sell-out price 38 elastic optimum 17 inelastic: raise to guardrail expected revenue impact +411,961 · contribution impact +557,859 validation queries: 6/6 passed Sample outputs are in sample_output/ . Some recommendations lower revenue while raising contribution. The model maximises contribution, and the output shows both numbers so the trade-off is visible.

docs.title: Produce pricing: elasticity, constrained price optimization & handover - Handover structure (what the next owner gets)
docs.text: 1. Overview : what the model decides, what it doesn't, and who signs off. 2. Inputs and outputs : sales history, forecasts, volume and unit cost in; recommended price, reason, and revenue and contribution impact out. 3. Methodology : the three steps above, including each rule and why it exists. 4. Validation queries : run before every publish; an empty result means pass. 5. Runbook : how to rerun, where outputs land, and what to do when a check fails.

docs.title: SQL performance tuning: measured, explained and checked for correctness - Overview
docs.text: A benchmark on 1M clinic appointments and 2.5M status events: five slow-query patterns, each with query plans before and after, timings, and a check that the results didn't change, except where the old query was wrong. Tools: SQL (SQLite here; the same patterns apply to Snowflake and Oracle), query plans (EXPLAIN), indexing, Python, pytest The patterns come from tuning report queries in my professional work; the clinic tables and data are invented. python -m tunekit run builds the database (about 30 s), runs every case, and writes RESULTS.md with the full SQL, plans and timings. Pattern Before → after What changed

docs.title: SQL performance tuning: measured, explained and checked for correctness - Overview
docs.text: Function on an indexed column ( STRFTIME(ts) = '2025-03' ) 256 ms → 2.0 ms range predicate on the raw column: SCAN becomes SEARCH, and the covering index means the table is never read Latest status per appointment 332 ms → 132 ms composite covering index in (appointment_id, event_ts) order removes a per-row sort and table fetch. The window-function rewrite was slower (494 ms, measured), so the SQL stayed as it was. One scalar subquery per output column 437 ms → 48 ms four correlated subqueries per session become one join with conditional aggregation

docs.title: SQL performance tuning: measured, explained and checked for correctness - Overview
docs.text: Join fan-out "fixed" in the report 1,515 ms → 982 ms the old query overstated charges by 87% : appointments with several RESCHEDULED events were counted once per event. EXISTS asks the intended question. Join without a useful index 62 ms → 15 ms date index plus a composite covering index on the join key; same SQL, different physical design Timings are medians of three runs on one machine. The results file records the SQLite and Python versions used.

docs.title: SQL performance tuning: measured, explained and checked for correctness - How each case is checked
docs.text: bench.py runs each case on a clean slate. Indexes both versions may use are created first, the "before" query is planned and timed, the case's new indexes are added, then the "after" query is planned and timed. Results are compared row by row. A case either declares the results identical, or, like the fan-out case, declares that the old query was wrong, and the benchmark reports by how much.

docs.title: SQL performance tuning: measured, explained and checked for correctness - How each case is checked
docs.text: The tests ( tests/ ) run every case on a 30k-row database and assert the plan changes each case claims: SCAN → SEARCH, the sort disappearing, four correlated subqueries becoming none, the new covering indexes being used. Timing is never asserted in tests, because it depends on the machine. It is measured on the full run instead.

docs.title: SQL performance tuning: measured, explained and checked for correctness - What I take from this
docs.text: 1. Read the plan before rewriting. Every case starts from EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN , not from intuition. 2. Measure the rewrite you believe in. The window-function version of "latest status" looked cleaner and was slower. 3. Performance work finds correctness bugs. The fan-out join was slow and wrong. That's the most valuable finding here. 4. Separate SQL changes from index changes , so you know which one bought the speed-up and what it costs to keep.

docs.title: SQL performance tuning: measured, explained and checked for correctness - Run it
docs.text: bash cd professional-work/query-tuning pip install -r requirements.txt PYTHONPATH=src python -m tunekit run builds bench.sqlite on first run, then benchmarks PYTHONPATH=src python -m tunekit run --rows 200000 quicker pytest -q 10 tests on a small database

docs.title: Legacy report migration kit: Oracle → Snowflake translator, column audit & parity harness - Overview
docs.text: Tools for moving a clinic network's legacy Oracle reports onto a modern warehouse: a rule-based SQL translator that logs every change, an output-column audit that finds the cause of "merged" columns, a parity harness that explains every difference, and a migration-wave planner. Tools: SQL (Oracle, Snowflake, SQLite), Python (pandas), pytest The approach comes from report migrations in my professional work; the clinic reports, tables and data are invented.

docs.title: Legacy report migration kit: Oracle → Snowflake translator, column audit & parity harness - How I approach a migration
docs.text: 1. Inventory every report: owner, schedule, sources, consumers, criticality. 2. Rebuild the logic as a documented view, keeping business rules in one place. 3. Prove parity : same rows, same totals, and every difference explained before anyone switches. 4. Automate the run and the checks; alert on failures instead of leaving silent gaps. 5. Hand over with a short runbook so the report survives without me.

docs.title: Legacy report migration kit: Oracle → Snowflake translator, column audit & parity harness - The migration kit
docs.text: src/migrationkit does steps 1–3 on six invented legacy Oracle clinic reports in legacy/ . 1. Translate : translate.py is a rule-based Oracle → Snowflake translator. It works on masked SQL, so strings and comments are never rewritten, and it logs every change with its line number. Anything it can't translate safely is flagged for review instead of guessed. Oracle Becomes The trap it avoids DECODE(x, NULL, 'a', ...) CASE WHEN x IS NULL THEN 'a' ... CASE x WHEN NULL never matches. DECODE treats NULLs as equal, so a column-valued search becomes (x = s OR (x IS NULL AND s IS NULL)) .

docs.title: Legacy report migration kit: Oracle → Snowflake translator, column audit & parity harness - The migration kit
docs.text: a.id = b.id(+) LEFT JOIN b ON a.id = b.id comma joins become explicit INNER/LEFT joins in dependency order; sessions with no appointments are kept WHERE ROWNUM <= 10 ORDER BY d ORDER BY d LIMIT 10 + review flag Oracle picks the 10 rows before sorting, so the legacy "latest 10" report returned 10 arbitrary rows. Someone has to decide which result was intended. TRUNC(amount) unchanged + review flag numeric TRUNC is not date TRUNC NVL , NVL2 , ADD_MONTHS , TRUNC(date,'MM') , SYSDATE , FROM DUAL , MINUS , hints COALESCE , CASE , DATEADD , DATE_TRUNC , CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() , -, EXCEPT , removed

docs.title: Legacy report migration kit: Oracle → Snowflake translator, column audit & parity harness - The migration kit
docs.text: CONNECT BY , PRIOR , MERGE , ROWID , .NEXTVAL review flag rewritten by a person (for example as a recursive CTE) The translator also has a SQLite target . The tests use it to execute the translated reports on synthetic data and compare the results with an independent pandas implementation of Oracle semantics ( reference.py ). Each report must match exactly. That's how the suite proves the DECODE and outer-join rewrites are correct, not just that they look right.

docs.title: Legacy report migration kit: Oracle → Snowflake translator, column audit & parity harness - The migration kit
docs.text: 2. Audit output columns : columns.py finds the root cause of "merged" columns: unaliased expressions, whose engine-generated names change between databases, and duplicate output names such as d.session_id, b.session_id , which BI tools collapse into one. It then adds aliases: capacity_position: col 2: b.session_id duplicate output name 'session_id' (also column 1) - BI tools merge these col 4: SUM(DECODE(b.status, 'C', 0, b.units)) expression without alias - engine-generated name changes between databases col 6: NVL2(MAX(b.referrer_id), 'REFERRED', ...) implicit alias without AS - easy to break by editing; add AS The translated, re-aliased views are in migrated/ , each with its change log and any REVIEW items in the header.

docs.title: Legacy report migration kit: Oracle → Snowflake translator, column audit & parity harness - The migration kit
docs.text: 3. Prove parity : parity.py lines up the legacy extract and the new view on the business key. It reports missing, extra and duplicate rows, column totals, and a diagnosis for every differing value : rounding, NULL vs 0, formatting, a constant scale factor (units or currency), a constant date shift (timezone), or logic: investigate . The verdict is PASS, PASS_WITH_EXPLAINED (only accepted categories), or FAIL. $ python -m migrationkit parity verdict: PASS_WITH_EXPLAINED rows: legacy 1,260 · new 1,260 · only in legacy 0 · only in new 0 revenue 22 differences - null_vs_zero: one side has NULL where the other returns 0 (NVL/COALESCE default) - NULL on the legacy side revenue 1214 differences - rounding: rounding only (whole units or cents) In this demo the legacy extract came from an older query version without NVL on charge and was written to a file that rounded money. Both are differences you can explain and sign off, not bugs. A changed value of any other kind turns the verdict to FAIL.

docs.title: Legacy report migration kit: Oracle → Snowflake translator, column audit & parity harness - The migration kit
docs.text: 4. Plan the waves : inventory.py scores each report in inventory.yaml . Value comes from criticality, frequency and users. Effort comes from what the translator found in its SQL: automatic rewrites are cheap, review items and column problems are not. Reports nobody has opened in 90 days are proposed for retirement instead of migration.

docs.title: Legacy report migration kit: Oracle → Snowflake translator, column audit & parity harness - The migration kit
docs.text: bash cd professional-work/report-migration pip install -r requirements.txt PYTHONPATH=src python -m migrationkit translate legacy/ .sql - migrated/ .sql with change logs PYTHONPATH=src python -m migrationkit columns output-column audit PYTHONPATH=src python -m migrationkit parity legacy extract vs migrated view PYTHONPATH=src python -m migrationkit plan migration waves pytest -q 29 tests, incl. executing translated SQL

docs.title: Clinic data warehouse: layers, lineage, linting & data contracts - Overview
docs.text: A working mini-warehouse for a clinic network's appointment data: SQL models built in dependency order, a convention linter, data contracts and generated documentation, so everyone can see what feeds what and broken data can't reach a report quietly. Tools: SQL (SQLite here, written to port to Snowflake), Python (networkx, matplotlib), pytest, data modelling, data governance The techniques come from my professional work designing warehouse layers and conventions; the clinic data is invented. python -m whgov run builds 8 models from raw appointment feeds and checks 40 contracts.

docs.title: Clinic data warehouse: layers, lineage, linting & data contracts - Design
docs.text: Five layers with one job each, enforced by the linter rather than by memory: Layer Purpose May read from raw data exactly as received, never queried by reports (sources) stg clean, standardize and de-duplicate. Bad rows go to stg.rejected_rows with a reason code. raw core conformed entities and facts (sessions, daily appointments) raw, stg, core mart business logic (benchmarks, projections, plans) core, mart rpt report-shaped outputs with friendly columns mart

docs.title: Clinic data warehouse: layers, lineage, linting & data contracts - Models as code
docs.text: Each model in models/ is a single SELECT with a header that documents it and declares its contract: sql -- model: mart.session_plan -- grain: one row per open session -- column projected_final: projected net appointments at session -- test: unique(session_id) -- test: expression(projected_final BETWEEN net_appointments AND capacity) -- test: assert_empty(SELECT 1 WHERE (SELECT COUNT( ) FROM core.sessions WHERE is_open = 1) < (SELECT COUNT( ) FROM mart.session_plan)) WITH today AS ( ... )

docs.title: Clinic data warehouse: layers, lineage, linting & data contracts - Models as code
docs.text: - Dependencies are read from the SQL (FROM / JOIN / comma joins, excluding CTE names), not declared by hand, so the graph can't drift from the code. project.py builds the DAG, rejects cycles and unknown references, and materializes models in topological order. select="+mart.segment_curves" rebuilds a model and only its upstream. - Contracts ( contracts.py ): unique , not_null , accepted_values , expression , relationship (no orphans) and assert_empty for reconciliation checks, such as "published rows = open sessions" or "segment totals = plan totals". Every built column must also be documented, and every documented column must exist. - Generated docs ( docs.py ): CATALOG.md with a Mermaid lineage graph, row counts and test status for every model, plus the lineage charts in figures/ .

docs.title: Clinic data warehouse: layers, lineage, linting & data contracts - The linter
docs.text: lint.py masks comments and string literals, then checks each model: Code Rule Why WG001 no SELECT an upstream column change must not leak silently into reports WG002 every computed column has AS alias unaliased expressions get engine-generated names that differ between databases, the root cause of "merged" columns after a migration WG003 no comma joins a missing join condition becomes a silent cross join WG004 layer rules (table above) keeps business logic out of reports and raw data out of marts WG005 description, grain, owner and a unique(...) grain test a model nobody can describe can't be trusted

docs.title: Clinic data warehouse: layers, lineage, linting & data contracts - The linter
docs.text: WG006 no hard-coded dates the run date comes from raw.run_context , so reruns and backfills work WG007 file path = model name, snake_case aliases you can find any table's code from its name WG008 / WG009 no top-level ORDER BY ; upper-case keywords warnings: style and wasted work

The linter earned its place while this repo was being built: it flagged that stg.rejected_rows had no grain test.

docs.text: The raw feed is generated with known problems (re-sent events, messy codes, blank sessions, bad units, unknown event types). The tests check that staging rejects exactly those rows, fixes the fixable ones, and that clean + rejected = distinct raw events . Other tests break the data on purpose and confirm the contracts catch it.

docs.title: Clinic data warehouse: layers, lineage, linting & data contracts - Notes
docs.text: - Each layer is its own attached SQLite database, so layer.table names work like schemas. The same model files would run on a cloud warehouse with only dialect changes. - The marts use the same method as the clinic capacity planning project, written in SQL.
